prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks that brought frequency and time measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: B015 is the cleanest invention-plus-demonstration story on the shortlist. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift while keeping many atoms interrogated in parallel, and Ye's strontium work showed the stability and systematic control that made 10^-18 real rather than a promise. The result is unambiguous and measurable, has been reproduced and surpassed by several independent laboratories and species, and feeds directly into the redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and tests of constant variation and dark matter. It is a two-name prize with no forced exclusion among the credited names, which is rare on this list: B016 has five names for three places, B012 and B051 have four. The ballots show real convergence: four first places and four top-three rankings, from members with different specialities.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered control of single ions, and some would say the lattice clock is the next increment in a recognised line. Several other groups (SYRTE, PTB, JILA beyond Ye, ion-clock groups) built essential parts of the field and are not carried by the two names. It also draws first-place support from only atomic and precision-measurement specialists, while B017 has broader top-three support (five members) across condensed matter and other subfields, so my own enthusiasm is correlated with my field.

responses.point: Danielsson placed twisted bilayer graphene first, with a sharp Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction, a decisive experiment and a field that has opened up broadly, and put B015 only seventh, asking whether lattice clocks are already covered by the comb and ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I accept that B017 is the most broadly supported candidate and I rank it as my first alternative. But I do not think the overlap objection holds up for clocks. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles and the 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems; neither supplies the magic-wavelength condition that lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once with the lattice shift cancelled, and that is what delivered the 10^-18 regime. That is a separate invention with a separate figure of merit. I would concede that the case is weaker if the committee wants a prize for a new phase of matter rather than a new measurement capability.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B015 first as a clean instrument-driven advance with an unambiguous figure of merit, and judged B017 premature because the pairing mechanism is unresolved and waiting a few years could clarify its consequences.
responses.response: I agree on B015 and on the clarity of the figure of merit, but I want to qualify the support. Neither of us should treat opening agreement as evidence of merit; we are two experimentalists who like instruments with a number attached. On B017 I do not fully share the prematurity worry. The superconducting pairing mechanism being open does not weaken the discovery of correlated states and the prediction that preceded them, so I would not use it as a reason to delay. My reservation about B017 is rather the credit boundary: the experimental credit sits with a group, with early-career researchers such as Yuan Cao absent from the credited names, so the three-name trio is more arbitrary there than for B015.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B012) first as the architecture of superconducting processors, while flagging that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits makes an immediate second prize in that family hard to justify, and disclosed proximity to the field.
responses.response: I think the 2025 proximity point is a real argument against B012 now and I value that you raised it against your own first choice. Circuit QED is a distinct discovery, but a committee choosing this year has to weigh the family effect, and B015 does not have that problem. I would press one qualification on my side: the Girvin-versus-Blais question for the theory share shows that B012 has the same forced-exclusion difficulty as B016, whereas B015 does not. If the committee instead prefers quantum technology as the theme, I would see B012 as a reasonable later candidate, not this year.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked biomolecular condensates (B003) first, arguing that statistical-physics ideas now give a quantitative language for intracellular organisation, while noting the open question of disciplinary fit and which structures are truly liquid.
responses.response: I take the physics content seriously: surface tension, nucleation and active droplets are real statistical physics, and I am not the right judge of the biology. My difficulty is the one you name yourself, that whether all claimed condensates are genuine phases is still contested. Compared with a clock whose accuracy is checked by direct comparison of independent devices, the evidence that B003 settles its central claim is harder to evaluate, so I would want to hear from the colleagues who know the cell-biology literature before ranking it near the top.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a distinct step from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes or as an increment.

Whether the omission of other lattice-clock groups can be defended with a two-name prize, and whether priority among early lattice-clock experiments is as clean as I recall; I have not verified it independently.
Whether B017 should be preferred this year given its broader top-three support, depending on how the committee weighs maturity and credit boundaries for experimental teams.
The pending redefinition of the second could be read either as a reason to wait or as a reason to act.
statement.conflict_note: No direct tie to Katori or Ye is documented in my profile. Adjacent connections that a recusal discussion should consider: I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my doctoral period, and Hall's work on combs and precision spectroscopy is part of the lineage that B015 builds on, although Hall is not a candidate here; my own work in laser stabilisation and spectral-hole materials shares techniques with clock work. For other shortlisted topics, my quantum-memory and quantum-information research and my involvement in WACQT (superconducting qubits) and Deep Light Vision are close to B016, B011, B010, B012 and B029, so I would discount my views there, but no specific conflict is apparent for B015.
